plate_findings.evidence: dense consolidation of the right upper lobe

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Chest radiograph from a patient with inhalation anthrax; caption describes right upper lobe infiltrate and mediastinal widening. The mediastinal widening is a classic finding; right upper lobe infiltrate is not in the vocabulary. B: Contrast-enhanced chest CT from a patient with inhalation anthrax; caption explicitly describes consolidation, mediastinal adenopathy, and bilateral pleural effusions. Red arrows annotate findings. C: Follow-up chest radiograph from the same inhalation anthrax patient; caption describes progressive right lung infiltrates, which are not represented by a specific vocabulary key. D: Follow-up chest radiograph from the inhalation anthrax patient; caption describes increasing left pleural effusion, a recognized manifestation.

panels.figure_caption: Chest x-ray and computed tomographic scan images for a patient with inhalation anthrax, Minnesota, USA. A) On hospital day 1, the x-ray image revealed a right upper lobe infiltrate and widening of the mediastinum. B) On hospital day 2, computed tomographic scan of the chest with intravenous contrast showed dense consolidation of the right upper lobe, mediastinal adenopathy (small arrow), and bilateral pleural effusions (large arrows). C) By hospital day 4, progressive infiltrates in the right lung were present. D) By day 6, an increasing left pleural effusion was evident.
in_text_mentions: On hospital admission, the patient’s temperature was 37.3°C, blood pressure 148/72, pulse 100, respiratory rate 20, and room air oxygen saturation 89% (median 95%, range 65%–100%). The right lung base had diminished breath sounds and apical crackles. Laboratory tests (Table 1) and chest imaging (Figure 1) were performed. Blood samples for culture were obtained, and ceftriaxone (2 g) and azithromycin (500 mg) (Table 2) were administered intravenously (IV) for presumed community-acquired pneumonia (CAP).

On hospital day 2, the patient had increasing tachycardia and higher oxygen requirements. A computed tomographic scan of the chest revealed multiple abnormalities (Figure 1). A Bacillus species was isolated from blood cultures and sent to the Minnesota Department of Health Public Health Laboratory (MDHPHL) for identification, and IV ciprofloxacin was initiated. On hospital day 3, the patient’s condition continued to decline (Table 1). MDHPHL identified B. anthracis in the blood cultures, and meropenem and vancomycin were added to the treatment regimen.
